summary: Defines a new 6LoWPAN dispatch type for route-over networks. It first targets compression of RPL data packet information: the RPL Option and the source routing header, plus an IP-in-IP technique. It can be extended for other uses. Later RFCs update it.

plainLanguage.summary: The Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) can add several routing headers to IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPAN). This RFC defines shorter forms for those headers so packets use less space.

questions: how does rpl header compression work
subtitle: A compact 6LoWPAN format for carrying RPL routing information across low-power wireless links.

tldr.problem: Low-power wireless links carry small frames, while RPL packets may include source routes, packet information, and IP-in-IP headers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8138 defines 6LoWPAN Routing Headers (6LoRH) that compress source-route entries, RPL Packet Information, and an outer IPv6 header.
tldr.outcome: The compressed headers reduce packet size but assume network-wide support. RFC 8138 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9008, RFC 9035, and RFC 9914.

today: RFC 8138 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9008, RFC 9035, and RFC 9914. The unit metadata does not list a later RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Routing Headers Need Compression
sections.content:
Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) aim to conserve energy, and smaller transmissions help. The classical IEEE 802.15.4 physical layer limits a frame to 127 bytes, while RPL can add a source-routing header, RPL Packet Information (RPI), and IP-in-IP encapsulation.

RFC 8138 extends the 6LoWPAN adaptation layer with compressed representations for these routing artifacts. It introduces a 6LoWPAN Routing Header (6LoRH) format that can also be extended for additional uses.
sections.plainLanguage: Small wireless frames have limited room for routing information. This RFC defines shorter ways to carry several RPL headers in those frames.

sections.title: Dispatch Types and Header Placement
sections.content:
6LoRH uses Page 1 of the 6LoWPAN Paging Dispatch, selected by the value 11110001. Its dispatch patterns distinguish Elective headers (101xxxxx), which an unfamiliar node may skip, from Critical headers (100xxxxx), which an unsupported node must not ignore.

A 6LoRH must follow any Fragmentation or Mesh header and precede LOWPAN_IPHC. Chains are compressed in the same order as their uncompressed headers. The compressed IP-in-IP header goes last in its chain, and compressed source-route headers precede the compressed RPI.
sections.plainLanguage: Each compressed header has a defined position and type. Some unknown headers may be skipped, but a node must discard a packet with a Critical header type it does not support.

sections.title: Compressing and Forwarding Source Routes
sections.content:
An SRH-6LoRH encodes route hops in order. Types 0 through 4 carry each IPv6 address in 1, 2, 4, 8, or 16 bytes. The Size field represents the number of entries minus one, and a header can encode up to 32 hops; multiple headers can carry longer paths or different compression levels.

Unlike the uncompressed source-routing header, a router consumes its own first route entry instead of swapping addresses. The packet therefore gets smaller as it travels, but consumed route information is not recoverable. If strict source routing is required and the receiving router is not the current segment endpoint, it must drop the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The route is a list of addresses, and each router removes its own entry when the packet reaches it. This saves space, but the packet no longer contains the route entries already used.

sections.title: Compressing RPL Packet Information
sections.content:
The RPI-6LoRH is a Critical header of Type 5. It carries the RPI flags, an RPLInstanceID, and a SenderRank. The I flag indicates that the instance ID is omitted for Global Instance 0. The K flag indicates that SenderRank is represented in one byte by omitting its least significant byte; otherwise, it uses two bytes.

A non-RPL router that receives an RPI-6LoRH should drop the packet rather than skip the header. Forwarding it without interpreting the RPL instance information could cause the packet to be reintroduced into the wrong instance and form a loop.
sections.plainLanguage: The Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) uses this header to carry the network instance and sender rank in a compact form. It can omit values when the format signals a known value or a zero byte.

sections.title: Compressing the Outer IP Header
sections.content:
The IP-in-IP-6LoRH is an Elective Type 6 header that compresses an outer IPv6 header. That outer header is used when a router inserts routing information into a packet it did not originate. The compressed header carries a Hop Limit, which is decremented at each hop; the packet is dropped when the limit reaches zero.

A Length of 1 means the encapsulator address is omitted because it is a known router, such as the RPL root. A larger Length indicates that a compressed encapsulator address follows. The root address is used as the compression reference.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router adds routing information to another node's packet, this format can describe the outer IP header in fewer bytes. It still carries a hop limit so the packet cannot travel forever.

sections.title: Network Support and Security
sections.content:
The design assumes a homogeneous network: all nodes use this compression, or none do. It does not provide a way to discover whether the next hop supports 6LoRH. A node that expected a header but did not receive one, or received an unknown one, is expected to send a rate-limited ICMPv6 Parameter Problem message to the root and raise a management alert.

The RFC says the compressed form is logically equivalent to the corresponding inline form and is not believed to add a new threat. The security considerations of RFCs 4944, 6282, and 6553 still apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Every node on a path needs compatible settings because routers do not negotiate support as packets move. The RFC says the compression does not add a new security threat, while existing 6LoWPAN and RPL security guidance still applies.

items.label: SRH-6LoRH
items.desc: Each address uses the full 16 bytes.
